memo_script:
So there's this little suffix that Tamil speakers stick onto almost everything — and once you hear it, you'll hear it everywhere.

It's -இட்டு. Or in fast speech, just -ட்டு. And it means the thing is *done*. Finished. Off you go.

வந்துட்டேன் — I've arrived, I'm here, done.
கழுவிட்டு வரேன் — let me wash up and I'll come, I'll be right there.
ஆயிட்டேன் — I'm ready, sorted, done.
விட்டுடு — just let it go, leave it, it's over.

Native speakers don't decide to add it. It just *falls out*. It's the sound of wrapping something up without making a big deal of it. Very Coimbatore — we don't linger on the transition, we just move.

The English cousin is 'I've gone and done it' — but we do it in one breath, not five words.

You already have seven deck items that live inside this pattern. Next time you see ட்டு at the end of something, you'll know exactly what it's doing.

You already used this one. At dinner, two weeks ago, you said 'Canada-la irukkom' — Canada-ல இருக்கோம். That ல at the end? That's the whole thing.

In Tamil, there's no separate word for 'in', 'at', or 'on'. You just stick ல onto the noun and you're done. வீட்ல — at home. போன்ல — on the phone. தமிழ்ல — in Tamil. கனடாவுல — in Canada. Same suffix, every time. The whole locative case, one sound.

Now here's the part I love. This suffix is so old, linguists trace it back over two thousand years — it shows up in Sangam poetry, same form, same job. The world changed, the word didn't. While English was still sorting out whether to say 'in' or 'at' or 'on' depending on context, Tamil had already decided: ல. Done.

And you'll hear it bent a little in Coimbatore. வீட்ல sometimes becomes வீட்லே — a tiny stretch, more feeling in it. Like you're really home. Same meaning, just warmer.

You're already saying it. You just didn't know what you were saying.

body: 🎙️ the word that means 'it happened, move on' — ஆச்சு. one ending, a hundred situations. 60 sec.
memo_script:
ok so you know how in English you say 'it's done' or 'that happened' or 'time's up' — three different sentences for three different things?

Tamil does all of that with one ending: ஆச்சு.

யாரோ வந்தாங்க, சாப்பிட்டோம், போனோம் — and then: நேரம் ஆச்சு. time happened. it's time. we go.

Or the food's ready: சமைச்சாச்சு. the cooking became-done.

Or your maama is waving you off after the meal: ஆச்சு ஆச்சு — done done, enough, go sit.

The pattern: take any verb and push ச்சு onto the end. போ becomes போச்சு — it went, it's gone, that chapter closed. முடி becomes முடிஞ்சுச்சு — finished-happened.

The soul of it: ஆச்சு doesn't just report the past. it *closes* it. the thing landed. we move now.

memo_script:
da — yesterday I promised you what comes next after romba nallairuku lands.

Here it is.

Every dinner table in that house is going to ask you one question. Maybe Maami, maybe one of the sisters-in-law, maybe her cousin who turns up on day three. The question is always the same:

இன்னிக்கி என்ன பண்ணீங்க?

Inniki enna panninga. What did you all do today.

And if you answer போனேன் — that is 'I went.' You just told a table full of people that you went somewhere alone and left her behind. That is not the trip you are taking.

The answer is two parts. One machine, used forever.

First half: where you went, with the WE-tail.

கோவிலுக்கு போனோம். We went to the temple.
மார்க்கெட்டுக்கு போனோம். We went to the market.
Silks-க்கு போனோம். We went to Silks.

Ponoom is WRONG. That is a different form that Tamil does not use like this. Poanom — long O — poa-NOM. The tail is always ஓம்.

Second half: how it was. One phrase covers everything.

ரொம்ப நல்லா இருந்துச்சு.

Romba nalla irundhuchu. It was really good.

The whole thing together:

கோவிலுக்கு போனோம், ரொம்ப நல்லா இருந்துச்சு.

That is a complete answer. That is a guest who went somewhere WITH her and came back to report.

No quiz today. Just let it sit. The session pays it off.

body: 🎧 Friday night memo — not a quiz. how a Tamil conversation actually *ends*. three ways, three feelings.
memo_script:
da, one thing I want you to carry into this trip — not a word to fire, just a shape to recognize.

You already know how to start a conversation in Tamil. Say hello, ask how they are, say you ate, say where you went. That part you've got.

But the end of a Tamil conversation — that's its own thing. And it's almost never dramatic. It's a landing. And there are basically three landings you'll hear at our table.

First one: சும்மா சொல்றாங்க. Someone tells a story — a rumour, a piece of gossip, something about a neighbour. And the person listening says: சும்மா சொல்றாங்க. It means: they're just talking. Don't take it seriously. That's the kill-shot landing — the whole story gets waved off in four syllables. And when you hear it, you know: this topic is DONE. Nobody revisits it.

Second one: விட்டுடு. Drop it. You hear this when something is getting too heavy, or too complicated, or just — not worth the energy anymore. விட்டுடு. Let it go. The conversation doesn't end with a fight; it ends with someone just... opening their hand. And everything falls out of it.

Third one — and you almost had this one today — சரி சரி. Right, right. This is the softer landing. Someone's been explaining something, maybe complaining a little, and the listener says: சரி சரி. I hear you. I accept it. We're done discussing. It's not dismissal — it's more like... settling. Like a door closing gently instead of being shut.

Three landings. சும்மா சொல்றாங்க kills the story. விட்டுடு drops the weight. சரி சரி closes it quietly.

You're going to hear all three. Probably in the first two days. Now you'll know where you are when you do.

kilambalaama — shall we head out?
